lesson.title: Matrix shape and transpose

lead.text: A table of numbers is called a matrix. The numbers sit in lines of two kinds: rows go across and columns go down. Here is a matrix of prices in pounds. Each row is a shop, and each column is an item.

The first row says that shop 1 sells item 1 for 3 and item 2 for 8. The size of a matrix is its shape, written as rows × columns. This one has 3 rows and 2 columns, so its shape is 3 × 2. Always say the rows first. A 2 × 3 matrix and a 3 × 2 matrix are different shapes, even though they hold the same number of entries.

diagram.alt: A table of prices with three rows, one for each shop, and two columns, one for each item. One view marks row 1, one marks column 2, and one marks that the table has 3 rows and 2 columns, so its shape is 3 × 2.
diagram.caption: The price table. Rows run across and columns run down. The shape counts the rows first and then the columns.

lead.text: Count the rows first and then the columns, and write the shape in that order.

reveal.text: There are two rows and three columns, so the shape is 2 × 3. Rows always come first.

lead.text: Each number inside a matrix is called an entry. To point at one, give its row and then its column, counting both from 1. In the price matrix, entry (3, 1) is 9, because it sits in row 3 and column 1: the third shop's price for the first item. Entry (1, 2) is 8.

Row first and column second is the same order as the shape, and it is easy to reverse by accident. Entry (2, 1) is 5, in the second row and the first column, and it is a different number from entry (1, 2). When the matrix has a name such as A, entry (i, j) of A means the number in row i and column j.

diagram.alt: The price table with its rows and columns numbered from 1. One entry at a time is shaded: entry (3, 1) is 9, entry (1, 2) is 8, and entry (2, 1) is 5. The row number always comes first.
diagram.caption: Row first, then column. Entries (1, 2) and (2, 1) are different places and hold different numbers.

lead.text: Back to the timetable. Flipping it so that the days run down the side turns each row into a column. For a matrix this operation is called the transpose. The transpose of A is written Aᵀ, and its columns are the rows of A taken in order.

Entries travel with their rows. A number in row i and column j of A sits in row j and column i of Aᵀ. The price matrix has 3 rows and 2 columns, so its transpose has 2 rows and 3 columns. The shape swaps along with the entries.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows the price matrix beside its transpose. Choose a row on the left and follow it to the right, where it lies down as a column.

lead.text: Flipping swaps the two directions. Decide where each of the numbers 4 and 7 ends up.

reveal.text: The 7 periods moved from the side to the top. Flipping a table swaps rows and columns, which is what the transpose does.

steps.headline: Find the transpose of a 2 × 3 matrix with rows (1, 2, 3) and (4, 5, 6).

workedSteps.text: Row 1 becomes column 1, and row 2 becomes column 2.

steps.headline: Find entry (3, 2) of Aᵀ, where A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&4&-2\\3&0&5\end{pmatrix}$.

workedSteps.text: Transposing swaps the positions. Entry (3, 2) of Aᵀ is entry (2, 3) of A.
Read entry (2, 3) of A. Count rows and columns from 1.

lead.text: A matrix can be applied to a vector. Take one row of the matrix and multiply it by the vector in matching pairs. Then add the products. That is a dot product worked out once per row, and each row supplies one entry of the result.

Take the price matrix and the vector (1, 0). Row 1 gives 3 × 1 + 8 × 0 = 3, row 2 gives 5, and row 3 gives 9, so the result is (3, 5, 9). Each row of this matrix has 2 entries, and it pairs with a vector of 2 entries. Offer it a vector of 3 entries and the pairing runs out, because the rows have nothing for the third entry to meet.

afterFigure.text: In the picture the matrix has 2 columns, so the vector beside it has 2 entries. A matrix accepts a vector only when the vector has one entry for each of its columns.

lead.text: A has 2 rows and 3 columns, and A v pairs each row of A with v.

reveal.text: You matched the vector to a row of A. Each row is as long as the matrix has columns, so the vector needs exactly that many entries.

lead.text: A shop chain keeps its sales in a table. Each row is a shop and each column is a day.

lesson.orientation: Read rows and columns, transpose entries and check input dimensions.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A school timetable has 4 days across the top and 7 periods down the side. Each box holds a lesson, and you find any lesson by choosing a day and a period. A teacher who prefers the days down the side can flip the whole sheet, so that rows become columns and columns become rows.

Tables of numbers turn up all over this subject. A table holds several vectors side by side, and one table can describe how a whole plane is stretched or turned. Before we use one we need to read it properly. That means knowing how big it is and how to point at a single number in it, and what flipping does to it.
This lesson turns the timetable into numbers. We name a table's size and flip it. We also find out which vectors a table fits.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find any number in a table by its row and column, and flip the table with the transpose.

recap.keyIdea: A matrix is a table with a shape of rows by columns. Its transpose swaps the two: entry (i, j) moves to position (j, i).

blocks.text: Back at the timetable, you can now say how big a table is and flip it. You found entry (3, 2) of Aᵀ and saw that applying a matrix to a vector needs one vector entry for each column.

recap.nextHook: Applying a matrix to a vector, as on the last screen, is more than arithmetic. The next lesson shows that it moves every point of the plane, and that the columns of the matrix decide where each point goes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The 7 periods move from down the side to across the top.

questions.prompt: A timetable has 4 days across the top and 7 periods down the side. You flip it so that the days run down the side. How many periods run across the top of the flipped timetable?
hints: Which direction do the periods run in the original timetable?
Flipping swaps the across and down directions.
The periods move from the side to the top. How many are there?

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of days. In the flipped timetable they run down the side.

questions.onCorrect: 7. Flipping a table swaps which way each label runs. A matrix transpose does just that.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It has 2 rows and 3 columns, so its shape is 2 × 3.

questions.prompt: What is the shape of the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}5&6&7\\8&9&0\end{pmatrix}$?
hints: Count the rows first, then the columns.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the shape of its transpose. Count rows first, then columns.
That counts all the entries. Shape is the number of rows by the number of columns.

questions.onCorrect: Rows first, then columns: 2 rows and 3 columns make shape 2 × 3.

questions.prompt: A has 2 rows and 3 columns. How many entries must v have for A v to make sense?
hints: Each row of A pairs up with v, entry by entry.
How many entries does one row of A have?
A row is as long as the matrix has columns.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A has three columns, so each row has three entries and v needs three entries.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of rows. Each row has as many entries as there are columns.

questions.onCorrect: Each row of A pairs with v entry by entry, so v needs one entry per column.

acceptedIdeas: Transposing swaps each entry's row and column.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Row i becomes column i, so every entry swaps its row and column.

questions.prompt: Why does entry (2, 3) of A end up at position (3, 2) in Aᵀ?

choices.label: Transposing swaps each entry's row and column.
Transposing reverses the order of all the entries.
Transposing changes the sign of each entry.

hints: Which of the two numbers in the position does the transpose change?

misconceptions.feedback: Reversing everything would also change the row. The transpose keeps each entry and swaps only its position's two numbers.
The entries stay as they are. Only their positions change.

questions.onCorrect: Row i becomes column i, so each entry's row and column numbers swap.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&4&-2\\3&0&5\end{pmatrix}$, what is entry (3, 2) of Aᵀ? Count from 1.
hints: Swap the two positions.
Entry (3, 2) of Aᵀ comes from entry (2, 3) of A.
Look in the second row and the third column of A.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Entry (3, 2) of Aᵀ is entry (2, 3) of A, which is 5.

misconceptions.feedback: That is entry (2, 2) of A. Swap the two positions as written.
That is entry (1, 2) of A. Swap the positions, then read the row and column.

questions.onCorrect: Swap the positions: entry (3, 2) of Aᵀ is entry (2, 3) of A.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&4&-2\\3&0&5\end{pmatrix}$, how many columns does Aᵀ have?
hints: Rows of A become columns of Aᵀ.
Count the rows of A.
The number of rows of A is the number of columns of Aᵀ.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A has two rows, so Aᵀ has two columns.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of columns of A. The transpose swaps rows and columns.

questions.onCorrect: A has two rows, and each becomes a column of Aᵀ.

questions.prompt: For the sales table A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&4&-2\\3&0&5\end{pmatrix}$, how many shops are there?
hints: Each row is a shop.
Count the rows.
Rows run across the matrix.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are two rows, and each row is a shop.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of days, which are the columns.

questions.onCorrect: Each row is a shop, so the number of rows is the number of shops.

questions.prompt: Let B = $\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\7&3\\4&0\end{pmatrix}$. What is entry (2, 1) of Bᵀ? Count from 1.
hints: Swap the two positions.
Entry (2, 1) of Bᵀ comes from entry (1, 2) of B.
Look in the first row and the second column of B.
